memoryText: Do not fear, for those who are with us are more than those who are with them.
readingInstruction: No new reading today. Read 2 Kings 6:16 slowly, several times, and then say it from memory. Read the meditation and the week in review, and choose one of the three questions to write about, pray over, or share with someone.
memoryVerseMeditation:
Elisha says these words to his terrified servant, who has just woken up to find an enemy army surrounding the city. They are among the most comforting words in the Old Testament.

“Do not fear.” This is one of the most common commands in the Bible. It is not a shallow instruction to stop feeling afraid. It comes with a reason. The servant had every reason to be afraid. The army was real. The danger was real. But the command rests on something he could not yet see.

“For those who are with us.” Elisha says “us.” He includes himself and his servant, and he points to a company that has not been introduced. Throughout Scripture, God’s people are surrounded by unseen allies. Angels minister to the heirs of salvation (Hebrews 1:14). The host of heaven is real.

“Are more than those who are with them.” It is a statement of comparison. The enemy has numbers, but the people of God have more. It is not a promise that nothing bad will happen, but that, in the end, no enemy can overpower the LORD’s side.

Then Elisha prays, “O LORD, please open his eyes that he may see.” The servant looks again, and the hills are full of horses and chariots of fire. Nothing in the situation changed except the servant’s sight. Faith is not pretending the army isn’t there. It is seeing that there is something greater.

For the Christian, the greater presence is the LORD himself. “If God is for us, who can be against us?” (Romans 8:31). “He who is in you is greater than he who is in the world” (1 John 4:4). When you feel surrounded, ask God to open your eyes.
weekInReview: This week you read the healing of Naaman and the greed of Gehazi, the siege of Samaria lifted by four lepers, and Elisha’s vision of the chariots of fire. You read Psalms 44 and 60, the laments of a people who feel rejected by God, and the confidence that vain is the salvation of man. You saw the fall of the house of Ahab at the hand of Jehu, whose zeal was partial, and the near end of David’s line under Athaliah, thwarted by Jehosheba and Jehoiada. And you saw that God keeps his people for the sake of his covenant with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob. The week taught that God uses the small and the outcast, that unbelief is costly, and that God preserves his promises through hidden faithfulness.
reflectionQuestions: Naaman nearly missed his healing because the remedy seemed too simple. Where are you tempted to resist grace because it comes in a form you did not expect?
God hid the line of David in the temple for six years. How does that encourage you when God’s promises seem hidden or delayed? How does Christ, the true son of David, fulfill them?
The four lepers said, “This day is a day of good news,” and told others. Who needs to hear good news from you this week?
prayerPrompts: Ask God to open your eyes to see those who are with you.
Thank him for his covenant faithfulness.
Rest in Jesus, the true son of David.
